transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Well, hi Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I, uh, I guess what brings me in is... well, I'm retired now, so I spend a good amount of my time over at the local museum. It gets me out of the house, keeps me busy, you know? But there's this thing that keeps happening, and it's just getting so frustrating. 

For example, the folks at the museum will be talking right to me—like, standing right in front of me—about the next art walk we're putting together. And it's a big deal, we have to coordinate a lot of things for it, so there are a lot of details. Anyway, they'll be talking, and I’ll be looking right at them, making eye contact, nodding, thinking I'm completely tuned in. But then... I realize I completely missed the middle of what they just said. It's like my brain just turned off the audio for ten seconds. 

And then I have to stop them, feeling like an absolute fool, and ask them to run it by me all over again. I mean, I'm looking right at them, but the words just drift right past me. It's embarrassing, to be honest, because I don't want them thinking I don't care about the art walk or that I'm ignoring them, because I really do care, it's just... I don't know why I can't seem to hold onto what people are saying right to my face.
When did you first start noticing these episodes where your mind seems to drift off during conversations?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask about when it started, because I've been thinking about that a lot lately. I mean, maybe I've always been a little bit of a daydreamer, but it really started becoming a genuine problem—like, noticeably causing trouble for me—about two years and four months ago. I remember the timeline pretty clearly because, well, it was right around the time my good friend Charlie passed away. 

Charlie and I used to handle all the museum liaison duties together. We were a real team, you know? He was the organized one, always had a little notebook with him, keeping track of every little detail, and I was more of the ideas guy, I guess. But when he died... well, it was a terrible loss, just awful. And suddenly, I was the one who had to take over all those duties by myself. All the coordinating, all the meetings, all the little moving parts for the art walks and the exhibits. 

And that's when I really started to notice it. Without Charlie there to catch the things I missed, or to sort of anchor the conversations, I realized just how much I was drifting off. I'd be sitting in these planning meetings, and suddenly I'm the only one taking notes, but I can't even write anything down because I just lost the last two minutes of the conversation. So yeah, two years and four months, give or take. It's just been me flying solo since then, and it's been... well, it's been a real struggle to keep my head in the game without him.

Since Charlie passed away two years ago, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling sad, empty, or down most days? Or have things you used to enjoy, like the museum work itself, stopped being as enjoyable?

Well, no, not really. I mean, of course I was sad when Charlie passed. Anyone would be, right? We were friends for a long time, and you don't just brush that off. The first few months were tough, I won't lie. I missed him terribly, missed our routine, missed just having him around to bounce ideas off of. But as for feeling sad or empty most days now? No, I wouldn't say that. 

And the museum... I still love the museum. I really do. It's my favorite place to be. I love the art, I love the history, I love the people who come in. I mean, just last week we had this group of third graders come through, and seeing their faces light up when they saw the dinosaur exhibit—even though it's a small exhibit, mostly just casts, but still—it just reminds me why I do it. I still get a kick out of planning the art walks, too. The actual work of it, the ideas, the creativity... that's still wonderful. 

It's just the... the execution part that's getting to me. The meetings, the talking, the trying to hold onto all the details when people are speaking to me. That's the part that's frustrating. But it's not because I don't enjoy it anymore. If anything, I want to do a good job because I care about it so much. It's just that my brain doesn't seem to want to cooperate when it comes to listening to the nitty-gritty stuff. So no, I wouldn't say I'm depressed or anything like that. Just... easily derailed, I suppose.

Besides having trouble following conversations, have you noticed any problems with your memory in other situations—like remembering appointments, names of people you've met, or things you've read or watched?

Well, memory... see, that's the tricky part, because I don't think it's my memory, exactly. I mean, I remember appointments fine, and I know everyone's name at the museum—even the new volunteers, like Sarah and David who just started last month. But reading... oh boy, reading has become a whole ordeal. 

I'll sit down with a new gallery packet—you know, the informational packets they give us whenever a new exhibit rotates in, which is usually every three months or so. They're usually about ten, maybe fifteen pages long, full of historical context, artist biographies, all the things we need to know to answer questions from the public. And I want to read it, I really do. So I sit down in my favorite chair by the window—the one with the good reading lamp, because my eyes aren't what they used to be—and I start reading. 

And for the first few minutes, I'm doing great. I'm taking it all in. But then... it's the strangest thing. My eyes will keep moving across the page, line by line, right down to the bottom of the page. I'm physically reading the words. But my mind? My mind is completely gone. I'll be thinking about whether I need to pick up milk on the way home, or remembering a documentary I watched last week about the Roman Empire, or wondering if the museum's HVAC system is going to hold up this summer because it was making a funny noise on Tuesday. 

And then I get to the end of the page, and I realize I have absolutely no idea what I just read. Nothing. It's like the words just bounced off my eyeballs. So I have to flip back and read the exact same part all over again. Sometimes I have to read the same paragraph three or four times before it actually sticks in my brain. It turns a twenty-minute reading task into an hour-long project. And it's not that I forgot what I read, it's that I never really read it in the first place, even though I was looking right at it. Does that make sense? It's just so aggravating, having to constantly backtrack like that.

Have you noticed any confusion about where you are, what day it is, or difficulty finding the right words when you're speaking? Or have you had trouble remembering things from your past, like events from years ago or people you've known for a long time?

Well, no, not at all. I mean, I always know where I am and what day it is. Like today, I know exactly what day it is because it's trash day in my neighborhood, and I always have to remember to drag the bins out to the curb before eight o'clock, otherwise the truck just breezes right past. And my past? Oh, my past is clear as a bell. I can tell you all about when I was a kid growing up, or the time I spent working at the hardware store before I retired. I remember the people, the places, all of it. I was just telling one of the new museum volunteers—David, I think I mentioned him earlier—about this trip I took to the Grand Canyon back in 1985. I remember the heat, the color of the rocks, the exact make and model of the rental car we had. A blue Ford Taurus, if you can believe it. 

And as for finding the right words... no, I don't think I have any trouble with that. I mean, I like to talk, as you can probably tell! I've always been a bit of a talker. My wife, God rest her soul, used to say I could talk the ear off a brass monkey. I never find myself grasping for a word or forgetting what an object is called. It's really just the focusing part, the staying tuned in when I'm supposed to be listening or reading. But my memory of who I am, where I am, and what I've done with my life? That's all perfectly intact, thankfully. It's just the present moment that seems to slip away from me sometimes, you know? Like I'm here, but my brain decides to take a little vacation without telling me. But no confusion, no. Just... distraction, I guess you'd call it.

When you're doing something you really enjoy—like looking at artwork at the museum or working on a project that excites you—do you still have these same problems with your attention drifting away, or does it seem to happen mainly during the meetings and coordination tasks that feel more like work?

Well, you'd think if I enjoy it, it would be a breeze, right? And for some things, it is. If I'm just walking through the gallery, looking at the paintings, or chatting with the visitors, I'm right there in the moment. I could do that all day without a single problem. But... well, when it comes to the behind-the-scenes work, even for the stuff I really love, it's a different story. 

Like, if I know I need to read through one of those long exhibit descriptions I mentioned earlier, or if I have to sit down and actually plan out a talk for one of the art walks... oh boy. I mean, I want to do it, I really do, because the subject matter is fascinating to me. We have this impressionist exhibit coming up—Monet, Degas, just beautiful, beautiful pieces—and I'm thrilled about it. But the thought of actually sitting down at my desk and forcing my brain to do all that organizing and heavy lifting? It honestly feels like pulling teeth. 

So what happens is, I'll be at home, and I'll say to myself, 'Okay, time to plan the talk.' But before I sit down, I'll suddenly decide that the baseboards in the hallway absolutely need to be wiped down right that very second. Or I'll go to the kitchen for a glass of water, notice a cabinet door is slightly crooked, and decide I have to go out to the garage to find my screwdriver—the yellow-handled Phillips head, not the flathead—to fix it. And while I'm out in the garage, I might as well sweep up the leaves that blew in under the door on Tuesday. 

I just keep finding all these little chores around the house to do first. I'll reorganize the junk drawer, I'll water the plants, I'll do absolutely anything to put it off. And it's not because I don't care about the art walk! It's just because sitting with all that reading and trying to string a cohesive plan together takes so much mental energy that I just... I run away from it, I guess. I avoid it as long as I possibly can, until I absolutely have to get it done.

Have you had any medical events or health changes around the time these attention problems started—things like head injuries, infections, surgeries, or has your doctor ever checked your blood pressure, thyroid, or done any blood work to rule out medical causes?

Well, no, nothing like that at all. I've actually been pretty lucky in the health department, knock on wood. I mean, sure, my knees get a little stiff when it rains, and I take a little pill for my cholesterol every morning, but as far as big medical events? No. No head injuries, never been knocked out or anything like that. And surgeries... well, I had my tonsils out when I was seven years old, but I'm pretty sure that doesn't count for what you're asking! No bad infections, either. 

And my regular doctor—Dr. Henderson over at the clinic on Elm Street, I've been seeing him for, gosh, must be fifteen years now—he keeps a pretty close eye on all my numbers. I go in every October for my annual physical, right before flu season so he can make sure I get my flu shot while I'm sitting right there in the exam room. He does the whole workup. Draws the blood, checks the thyroid, does the blood pressure cuff, all of it. He prints out this little chart with all the results for me to take home. 

And every single time, he tells me I'm doing just fine for a guy my age. My blood pressure is usually right where it should be. Sometimes it's a tiny bit high if I've had too much coffee that morning—I like a good strong cup of Folgers with my breakfast—but nothing he's ever been concerned about. All the blood work always comes back clean as a whistle. Thyroid is perfectly normal. So, no, there haven't been any sudden health changes or medical issues that popped up out of nowhere. It's really just this... this frustrating business with my focus that we've been talking about. Physically, the engine is still running just fine, it's just the steering wheel that seems to get a little loose, if that makes sense.
Over the past two years, have you noticed any changes in how much you sleep at night, or changes in your appetite—like eating more or less than you used to?

Sleep and appetite? Well, let me think... no, no, I wouldn't say there's been any change there at all. I've always been a real creature of habit, you see. Especially when it comes to my sleep. Ever since I retired from the hardware store, I've kept to pretty much the exact same schedule. I usually head up to bed right after the ten o'clock local news—I watch Channel 4, mostly because I like their weatherman, he always has a little joke at the end of the broadcast that gives me a chuckle. Anyway, I head up, brush my teeth, and once my head hits the pillow, I might toss and turn for maybe five minutes just trying to get the blankets right, but then I'm out like a light. 

I sleep straight through until about six-thirty every single morning. I don't even need to set an alarm clock anymore, my body just naturally knows when it's time to get up. I've never been one of those folks who wakes up at three in the morning staring at the ceiling, tossing and turning. My wife used to joke that I could sleep through a marching band practicing right there in our living room. So, no, sleep is perfectly fine, hasn't changed a bit. 

And as for my appetite... well, that's just as steady as ever, too. I don't eat quite as much as I did when I was a younger man, of course, but over the last two years? Not a bit of difference. I still have my usual breakfast every morning—two eggs over easy, a piece of whole wheat toast with just a little pat of butter, and that strong cup of Folgers I mentioned earlier. Lunch is usually just a sandwich, maybe turkey and Swiss on rye, and then I make myself a sensible dinner. I do all my own cooking now, which mostly means keeping it simple so I don't make too many dirty dishes, but I never skip a meal. 

I definitely haven't lost any weight, and I haven't gained any either. In fact, my belt has been on the exact same notch for, oh, it has to be at least five or six years now. The leather is even getting a little worn down right at that specific hole! So, no, my sleeping and eating are right as rain. It's really just the... the mental wandering, the putting off the paperwork and getting distracted by the baseboards and the crooked cabinet doors, like I was telling you. The physical stuff is all holding steady.

When you're actually at the museum looking at the artwork or talking with the visitors—not the planning part, but the actual enjoyment of it—do you find that you still get genuine pleasure from it the way you used to, or does it feel kind of flat or empty now?

Oh, goodness no! No, not flat or empty at all. If anything, I might enjoy it even more now than I did when I first started volunteering. It's really the highlight of my week. When I'm actually out there on the floor—walking those beautiful old hardwood floors they have in the east wing, you know the ones that squeak just a little bit right near the gallery entrance?—I just feel this immense sense of... well, joy, I suppose you'd call it. 

I mean, just last Thursday, we had this group of middle schoolers come through on a field trip. Usually, kids that age, they're looking at their phones or poking each other, but I got to talking to this one young man about a landscape painting, explaining how the artist used light and shadow to draw your eye right to the little farmhouse in the corner, and his eyes just lit up. Seeing that? Oh, it fills my cup right to the brim. It really does. 

I could stand there for hours just soaking it all in and chatting with folks about the history of these pieces. There's this one sculpture in the atrium, a bronze piece of a heron taking flight, and every time the afternoon sun hits it around three o'clock, it just takes my breath away, exact same as the very first time I saw it years ago. So, no, the pleasure is absolutely still there, a hundred percent. It's just the paperwork and the sitting at the desk trying to organize the schedules that gets me all tangled up. But the art itself? And the people? Oh, I wouldn't trade that for the world. It's just wonderful, truly wonderful.

When you're thinking about sitting down to do that planning work or read through those exhibit packets, before you actually start avoiding it—do you notice any feelings of anxiety, dread, or worry? Like, does the thought of doing it make you feel tense or uncomfortable in your body?

Anxiety? Dread? Well, let me think on that for a second... no, no, I wouldn't use those words at all. I don't feel scared or worried about reading through the packets, and I definitely don't get any kind of physical tension. My stomach doesn't tie up in knots, my shoulders don't get stiff... nothing like that. It's actually quite the opposite, really. 

When I decide it's time to sit down and do the planning, I'll go into the spare bedroom—we turned it into a little home office after our youngest moved out to Omaha, just put a nice rug in there and painted it a very soothing shade of blue—and I'll sit down at my desk. It's this beautiful old oak roll-top desk I picked up at an estate sale back in '98, though the bottom left drawer does stick a bit when the humidity gets high. Anyway, I'll sit there in my chair, feeling perfectly fine, perfectly comfortable. I'll pull the exhibit packet out, set it right in the middle of the desk, and I just... well, I just don't start. 

There's no worry or panic about it. It's not like I'm sitting there sweating, thinking, "Oh gosh, I can't do this." It's more like my brain just says, "You know what? Let's look out the window instead." Or I'll notice that my pencils aren't perfectly sharp, so I'll get up to sharpen them. And the next thing I know, I'm standing by the window watching the neighbor's bird feeder because the squirrels have figured out how to bypass the baffle they put up. Clever little things, those squirrels, they'll hang upside down by their back toes just to get at the sunflower seeds! 

But no, to get back to what you were asking, as far as feeling tense or dreading the work? Not at all. I know I can do the work, and it certainly doesn't frighten me. I don't feel uncomfortable in my body one bit. I just end up doing absolutely everything else in the room except the paperwork.
Has your regular doctor—Dr. Henderson—ever done any brain imaging like an MRI or CT scan, or referred you to a neurologist for any reason?

Brain imaging? Oh, no, no. Dr. Henderson hasn't ever ordered anything like that for me. No MRIs or CT scans or... what was the other one? A neurologist, right, no, I've never been sent to one of those either. 

I've been seeing Dr. Henderson for, oh, it has to be fifteen years now. Ever since old Dr. Miller retired and moved down to Florida—Tampa, I think it was, or maybe Clearwater, somewhere on the Gulf side. Anyway, Dr. Henderson took over the practice, and he's a very thorough fellow, always takes his time with you. But for me, it's always just been your standard, run-of-the-mill checkups. You know, he listens to my heart, checks my breathing, taps my knees with that little rubber hammer. He does run my blood work every year right around my birthday in October, mostly just to keep an eye on the cholesterol, because my dad had a bit of trouble with his later in life. But my numbers have always come back right in the sweet spot. 

As for my brain, though? No, he's never felt the need to look in there. I've never had any fainting spells or terrible headaches or anything physical like that that would make him want to send me to a specialist. My wife, now, she had to get an MRI on her knee a few years back when she slipped on some ice out by the mailbox—it was one of those sneaky black ice patches you can't see until you're already going down—and she said it was terribly loud in that machine. She said it was like being stuck inside a tin can with somebody banging on the outside with a wrench! So I have to say, I'm quite glad I've never had to go through one myself. But to answer your question, no, strictly routine physicals for me, nothing at all having to do with brain scans or neurologists.

Have you ever experienced any episodes where you felt like you were watching yourself from outside your body, or felt like things around you weren't quite real—like you were in a dream or watching a movie of your own life?

Outside my body? Like... floating up near the ceiling looking down at myself? Oh, goodness no. No, nothing like that at all. I've heard of people having things like that happen when they're in surgery or something, near-death experiences they call them, I think? You see it on those television programs sometimes. But no, I've never had anything even close to that. I am very much firmly planted right here in my own shoes. Sometimes I wish I could float outside my body, especially when my lower back gets stiff! It usually gets me right down the left side, especially if I've been standing too long on those hard museum floors we were talking about earlier, but no... I'm always just right here, being me. 

And as for feeling like things aren't real, or being in a movie... no, I can't say I've ever felt that way either. My life wouldn't make a very exciting movie anyway, I don't think! Mostly just me puttering around the house, watching the birds, doing my volunteer work... though I suppose they make movies out of less these days. My wife, she watches those movies on the Hallmark channel, you know the ones, especially around Christmas time. They always seem to have the exact same plot—some big-city businesswoman goes to a small town and falls in love with a fellow who owns a Christmas tree farm or a bakery. We must have watched a dozen of them last December. I always tease her about it, I'll say, "Martha, you know how this one ends before the opening credits are even finished!" But she just likes how cozy they are, and I suppose there's no harm in that. It's nice to have something predictable.

But no, my own life? It feels perfectly real to me. The coffee tastes like coffee, the cold wind feels cold... I never get confused about whether I'm awake or dreaming. I do have some pretty vivid dreams sometimes, mind you. Just the other night I dreamt I was trying to fix the lawnmower, but instead of a spark plug, it needed... oh, what was it... a pendulum from a grandfather clock! Isn't that funny how the brain just throws things together like that while you're sleeping? But the moment I open my eyes and see the morning light coming through those floral curtains Martha picked out for the bedroom, I know exactly where I am. Everything is completely real. So no, no out-of-body experiences or movie-feelings for me.

You mentioned that when you're at the museum looking at the artwork or talking with visitors, you feel that joy and focus is there. But I'm curious—when you're doing something you truly enjoy at home, like maybe a hobby or something that really captures your interest—do you find that same ability to focus and stay present, or do you still struggle to keep your attention even on things you genuinely want to be doing?

Well, that’s a very interesting question, Doctor, because you’d think if I enjoy something, it would just be a breeze to stick with it, right? But it’s actually not quite that simple. Take the museum work we were just talking about, for instance. I absolutely love being there on the floor, talking to the visitors and pointing out the details in the artwork. But to do that well, I have to do a fair bit of reading at home to prepare. 

The head curator, Susan—lovely woman, she’s been there for going on twenty years now and knows absolutely everything there is to know about local history and the visiting artists—she gives us these gallery packets and sets of notes whenever a new exhibit comes in. And I genuinely want to read them. I really do! I find it all fascinating, especially the background on how the artists lived. 

So, I’ll take the packet home, and I’ll sit down in my favorite armchair in the living room. It’s this big brown leather recliner Martha got me for our anniversary a few years back, incredibly comfortable, maybe almost too comfortable sometimes. I’ll have my reading glasses on, a fresh cup of decaf on the side table, and I’ll open up the gallery packet or my notes. And I always start out just fine. For the first few minutes, I’m right there, completely engaged, taking it all in. 

But then... well, it’s the strangest thing. Even though I genuinely want to be reading it, after just a few minutes, my eyes will keep moving right over the page, scanning line after line, but my mind has just completely wandered off somewhere else entirely. I'll be looking right at the words, but my brain is suddenly thinking about whether I need to change the spark plug in the lawnmower, or wondering if it's going to rain later because my left knee is acting up, or trying to remember the name of that actor from the movie Martha and I watched last week. 

Meanwhile, my eyes are still doing the physical work of reading, going left to right, top to bottom. I won't even realize it’s happened until I get to the bottom of the page, and suddenly it dawns on me that I haven't actually taken in a single word for the last three paragraphs. The lights are on but nobody's home, as my dad used to say! So then I have to stop, sigh, find exactly where I lost the thread, and read the exact same part all over again. 

Just last week, we had this new exhibit on 19th-century pottery coming in, and I swear to you, I had to read the same paragraph about clay glazing techniques four times before it actually registered in my brain. So even with things I really enjoy and genuinely want to learn about, just sitting there and keeping my attention on the page... it’s quite a struggle. The focus just slips right away from me, no matter how much I want to hold onto it.

When you're doing something very familiar and automatic—like driving to the museum, or doing a task you've done hundreds of times before—do you find your mind drifting away like it does with the reading and planning, or does your attention stay pretty steady with those routine, practiced activities?

Driving to the museum... well, now that you mention it, that's a whole other story, isn't it? It's funny you bring up driving, because I've been taking that same route to the museum for... gosh, it has to be five years now. I take Elm Street down past the old high school, take a right on Maple, and then it's just a straight shot down Washington Avenue. I know every pothole, every stoplight, every place where the speed limit drops from 35 down to 25 right before you hit the school zone. 

And you know, because I know it so well, my mind just absolutely takes off. I'll get in the car, turn the key, maybe put on the classic rock station—though half the time I don't even really hear the music—and before I know it, I'm pulling into my spot in the museum parking lot, right next to Susan's little silver Honda. And I'll sit there for a second and think, "How on earth did I get here?" 

It's like I was completely on autopilot the whole way. My hands were steering, my feet were doing the pedals, I must have stopped at all the red lights because I didn't get into any accidents, thank heavens, but my mind? Oh, my mind was miles away. I'll be thinking about whether I need to pick up milk on the way home, or replaying a conversation I had with Martha the night before about whether we should finally get the gutters cleaned out—they get so clogged with those oak leaves in the fall, you know, it's a real mess when it rains—or I'll be trying to remember the name of that fellow who used to live next door to us back in the eighties. 

It happens with other things, too, not just driving. Like when I'm doing the dishes. Martha cooks, I clean, that's our arrangement, and it works out beautifully. I'll be standing there at the sink, scrubbing a pot, and my hands are just doing the work, right? Scrub, rinse, put it in the rack. But my brain is off trying to solve the world's problems, or just wandering down some random memory lane. I'll finish the whole stack of dishes and realize I wasn't present for a single second of it. 

So yes, when it's something I've done a million times, like driving that familiar route or doing the chores, my attention just packs its bags and goes on vacation. It doesn't stay steady at all. If anything, because the task is so automatic, it almost gives my brain permission to just wander off completely. It's a bit unsettling sometimes, really, especially with the driving, to realize you've just navigated a two-ton machine through traffic without really being conscious of it. But I suppose if I haven't hit anything yet, my autopilot must be pretty good!
Have you ever had any head injuries, concussions, or times when you were knocked unconscious—even if it was many years ago, before Charlie passed away?

Knocked unconscious? Oh, my, no. No, thankfully I have managed to keep my head pretty well protected all these years. Even going way back, long before we lost Charlie, bless his heart, no, I have never had any concussions or anything severe like that. 

I mean, I have had my fair share of bumps and scrapes, just like any boy growing up, and of course as an adult doing things around the house. There was this one time, oh, gosh, it must have been a good fifteen years ago now. I was under the kitchen sink, trying to fix a leak in the pipe down there. Martha had been telling me for weeks to just call a plumber, but you know how it is, you want to try and fix it yourself to save a few dollars. Anyway, I was wedged under there, and the wrench slipped, and I jerked my head back and hit it right on the edge of the open cabinet door. It was a loud whack, I tell you. Oh, I saw stars for a minute, I really did. It sounded like a hollow melon hitting a concrete floor. Martha came running in from the living room, she was just frantic, insisting we needed to go straight to the emergency room. She even had her purse in her hand and the car keys ready to go. 

But I just sat there on the linoleum for a minute, rubbed it, and told her I was perfectly fine. I never lost consciousness, did not get dizzy or sick to my stomach or anything like that. I just ended up with a goose egg the size of a golf ball on the back of my head for about a week. I had to sleep on my stomach because it was so tender! But no concussion. 

And I never played tackle football or any of those rough sports when I was in high school, either. My mother was absolutely terrified of head injuries. She used to read these medical articles in magazines about people getting knocked out and she absolutely forbade it. I stuck to track and field, just running in a straight line, mostly, so there was not much chance of a concussion there unless you trip over your own two feet! So no, Doctor, my brain has not been rattled around like that. Just the usual everyday bumps, but never anything where I was knocked out or had a real head injury.

You mentioned that Charlie's death two years and four months ago was when these attention problems really started. In those first few months right after he passed, before the attention problems became noticeable, did you experience a period where things felt emotionally numb or disconnected—like you were going through the motions but not really feeling much of anything, even things that would normally matter to you?

Numb? No, I... no, I wouldn't say numb. Actually, it was quite the opposite for me. I know some folks talk about going into shock, where they just walk around like a zombie and don't feel a thing for months. Martha’s sister, Helen, she was exactly like that when her husband passed away back in the nineties. Just completely blank. But for me... no, I felt every single bit of it, right from the very second we got the news. 

It was like... well, it was like walking around with no skin on, if that makes any sense. Everything just hurt. I remember those first few weeks so clearly, which is funny considering how much trouble I have keeping my mind on a book these days. The house was just absolutely full of people, neighbors coming in and out, folks from the church bringing over casseroles—I swear to you, we had enough baked ziti and potato salad to feed the entire county, the refrigerator was just packed to the brim. And Martha, oh, my poor Martha was just inconsolable. 

And I was right there with her. I wasn't disconnected from it at all. I was crying right along with her at the kitchen table. We'd sit there at two in the morning, just the two of us, drinking chamomile tea because neither of us could sleep a wink, and we'd just hold each other and weep. target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of head injuries, concussions, or loss of consciousness, which is not covered by any of the symptoms in my profile.

patient.answer:
Knocked unconscious? Oh, my, no. No, thankfully I have managed to keep my head pretty well protected all these years. Even going way back, long before we lost Charlie, bless his heart, no, I have never had any concussions or anything severe like that. 

I mean, I have had my fair share of bumps and scrapes, just like any boy growing up, and of course as an adult doing things around the house. There was this one time, oh, gosh, it must have been a good fifteen years ago now. I was under the kitchen sink, trying to fix a leak in the pipe down there. Martha had been telling me for weeks to just call a plumber, but you know how it is, you want to try and fix it yourself to save a few dollars. Anyway, I was wedged under there, and the wrench slipped, and I jerked my head back and hit it right on the edge of the open cabinet door. It was a loud whack, I tell you. Oh, I saw stars for a minute, I really did. It sounded like a hollow melon hitting a concrete floor. Martha came running in from the living room, she was just frantic, insisting we needed to go straight to the emergency room. She even had her purse in her hand and the car keys ready to go. 

But I just sat there on the linoleum for a minute, rubbed it, and told her I was perfectly fine. I never lost consciousness, did not get dizzy or sick to my stomach or anything like that. I just ended up with a goose egg the size of a golf ball on the back of my head for about a week. I had to sleep on my stomach because it was so tender! But no concussion. 

And I never played tackle football or any of those rough sports when I was in high school, either. My mother was absolutely terrified of head injuries. She used to read these medical articles in magazines about people getting knocked out and she absolutely forbade it. I stuck to track and field, just running in a straight line, mostly, so there was not much chance of a concussion there unless you trip over your own two feet! So no, Doctor, my brain has not been rattled around like that. Just the usual everyday bumps, but never anything where I was knocked out or had a real head injury.

doctor.intent: Distinguish between a dissociative disorder (F48.9), major depressive disorder (F32.9), and a medical/neurological condition (F06.8) by determining if the patient has experienced any periods of significant emotional numbness, loss of interest, or depressive symptoms that would support F32.9, versus clarifying the timeline and nature of the attention/dissociative symptoms to rule out F06.8 (which would require a medical cause) and better characterize F48.9 (dissociative disorder NOS).
doctor.question: You mentioned that Charlie's death two years and four months ago was when these attention problems really started. In those first few months right after he passed, before the attention problems became noticeable, did you experience a period where things felt emotionally numb or disconnected—like you were going through the motions but not really feeling much of anything, even things that would normally matter to you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotional numbness or disconnection following the death of the patient's friend, which relates to symptoms of depression, grief, or trauma. The symptom profile does not contain information about emotional numbness or disconnection.

patient.answer:
Numb? No, I... no, I wouldn't say numb. Actually, it was quite the opposite for me. I know some folks talk about going into shock, where they just walk around like a zombie and don't feel a thing for months. Martha’s sister, Helen, she was exactly like that when her husband passed away back in the nineties. Just completely blank. But for me... no, I felt every single bit of it, right from the very second we got the news. 

It was like... well, it was like walking around with no skin on, if that makes any sense. Everything just hurt. I remember those first few weeks so clearly, which is funny considering how much trouble I have keeping my mind on a book these days. The house was just absolutely full of people, neighbors coming in and out, folks from the church bringing over casseroles—I swear to you, we had enough baked ziti and potato salad to feed the entire county, the refrigerator was just packed to the brim. And Martha, oh, my poor Martha was just inconsolable. 

And I was right there with her. I wasn't disconnected from it at all. I was crying right along with her at the kitchen table. We'd sit there at two in the morning, just the two of us, drinking chamomile tea because neither of us could sleep a wink, and we'd just hold each other and weep. I was the one making all the phone calls, talking to the funeral director—Mr. Higgins, very kind man, handled everything with such grace—and writing out the thank-you notes for all the flowers. We got so many lilies, the whole house smelled like a botanical garden for weeks. 

So, no, I didn't have that feeling of just going through the motions or being numb to the world. I was feeling everything, probably too much, really. It was just a heavy, heavy sadness that sat right on my chest. I was very present for all of that pain, unfortunately. The wandering mind, the losing my place in things, all that trouble paying attention... that all sort of crept in a bit later on, as the months went by. But right at the beginning? No, Doctor, there was no numbness at all. Just a whole lot of tears and heartbreak.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the attention problems represent a dissociative disorder (F48.9) with depersonalization/derealization features, or a neurocognitive issue (F06.8) potentially related to a past head injury, by asking about dissociative symptoms that would distinguish these from depression (F32.9)
doctor.question: You mentioned that when you're driving that familiar route to the museum, you sometimes realize you've arrived without remembering the drive itself—like your hands and feet were doing the work but you weren't really there. During those moments when you're on autopilot like that, do you ever feel like you're watching yourself from a distance, or like you're observing your own hands steering the wheel as if they belong to someone else?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of depersonalization (feeling like an outside observer of one's own body or actions), which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Watching myself from a distance? Oh, goodness, no. No, it’s nothing spooky like that. That sounds like something out of one of those science fiction programs Charlie used to watch on the television late at night. No, I don't feel like I'm floating outside the car or looking down at myself, and my hands definitely still feel like my own hands. In fact, I’m quite aware they’re mine because I've got a bit of arthritis starting up in this left thumb joint here, so they remind me they belong to me quite often, especially when it’s damp out! Martha actually bought me this wonderful sheepskin steering wheel cover last Christmas just to keep my hands warm on those chilly mornings, and I can feel that soft wool the whole time.

So, no, when I say autopilot, I just mean I am completely wrapped up in whatever I'm thinking about. I'm not disconnected from my body, I'm just... well, I'm just ignoring what my body is doing because my brain is so busy chewing on something else. Like, I'll be sitting right there in the driver's seat, feeling the heater blowing on my feet, but in my head, I'm trying to remember if I put the trash cans out on the curb, or I'm running through the grocery list trying to picture if we have enough coffee filters. 

Just the other day, I was driving along and I got completely caught up thinking about the lawnmower. It’s been making this terrible sputtering sound, and I was running through the steps in my head, trying to remember if I had the right socket wrench in the garage to check the spark plug, or if I had lent it to Dave from three houses down. Dave is absolutely terrible at returning tools, by the way. I lent him a power drill back before the pandemic and I still haven't seen hide nor hair of it. So I'm sitting there driving, but my mind is entirely focused on Dave, and the drill, and the spark plug. 

I'm still me, and I'm still right there inside my own head. It's just that my eyes are looking at the road, but my brain isn't bothering to process the road, if that makes sense. It's processing the lawnmower. So no, definitely no out-of-body experiences or feeling like my hands belong to a stranger. It's just plain old daydreaming, really... just a very, very deep daydream that takes up all my attention until I put the car in park and snap out of it.

This pattern, combined with avoidance of difficult tasks without anxiety, suggests adjustment disorder with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct (F43.25) or unspecified neurotic disorder (F48.9) rather than organic/medical etiology. doctor.question: When you're sitting down to read one of those gallery packets and your mind wanders off—in those moments, does it feel like you're choosing to let your mind wander because the task feels overwhelming or unpleasant, or does it feel more like your attention is just slipping away from you against your will, even though you genuinely want to stay focused?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I can sit down with a gallery packet or a set of notes and start out fine, but after a few minutes my eyes keep moving over the page while my mind has wandered off and I have to read the same part again.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's experience when their mind wanders while trying to read gallery packets, specifically whether they choose to let it wander or if attention slips away against their will. This directly relates to the difficulty in sustaining attention during tasks, which matches the manifestation of S002 where the patient describes trying to read a gallery packet but their eyes keep moving while their mind wanders off.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, I am certainly not choosing to let it happen. I genuinely want to read those packets! The museum director, Susan—lovely woman, always wears these bright, beautiful silk scarves—she puts so much effort into putting those notes together for us volunteers. So it's not that I find the reading unpleasant or overwhelming at all. I really, truly want to learn the material so I can be helpful to the visitors. 

I'll sit down in my recliner in the den, usually with a cup of decaf coffee—I have to switch to decaf after two o'clock in the afternoon nowadays or I will be staring at the ceiling all night long—and I'll have the gallery packet or a set of notes right there on my lap. And I start out just fine! I really do. I'll read the first paragraph or two and I'm right there, taking it all in, learning about the brushstrokes or the historical context or whatever it is. 

But then... well, it's exactly like you said, my attention just slips away from me entirely against my will. After just a few minutes, my eyes keep moving over the page, going line by line, left to right, just like they're supposed to. But my mind has completely wandered off somewhere else. I could be looking at a whole page about 19th-century watercolors, and my brain is suddenly thinking about whether I need to clean the gutters before the weekend rain, or if I remembered to put the damp towels in the dryer. 

And the most frustrating part is, I don't even realize it's happened until I get to the bottom of the page! I'll look down and think, 'What on earth did I just read?' Because not a single word of it actually stuck in my head. My eyes did all the work, but nobody was home to receive the message, if you catch my drift. So then I have to flip back and read the exact same part all over again. Sometimes I have to read the same paragraph three or four times before I can actually get it to stay in my brain. It’s terribly frustrating, Doctor, because I truly do want to stay focused, but my brain just won't cooperate with me once I've been sitting there for a few minutes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's attention difficulties represent a persistent inability to concentrate (consistent with F32.9 depression) versus episodic dissociative episodes where he loses time or awareness (consistent with F48.9 other specified dissociative disorder). Specifically, I need to clarify if his mind is simply wandering while he remains aware of his surroundings and the passage of time, or if there are gaps in his awareness where he loses chunks of time without knowing what happened.
doctor.question: When you're reading those gallery packets and your mind wanders off—afterward, when you realize you've lost the thread, do you remember sitting there the whole time, or are there gaps where you can't account for what you were doing or how much time passed?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about dissociative amnesia or memory gaps (losing time) during episodes of mind wandering, which is not covered by my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Gaps? Oh, heavens, no. No, no missing time or anything frightening like that. I remember sitting there the entire time. It's not like I wake up and wonder where the afternoon went, or... or like I've been abducted by aliens, you know? No, I'm fully aware that I'm just sitting right there in my brown leather recliner—the one I got at Macy's back in, oh, it must have been 2015, they were having a wonderful Presidents' Day sale and Martha insisted my old chair was ruining my posture. 

So I know exactly where I am and exactly what I'm doing. And I know exactly how much time is passing, too. We have this beautiful grandfather clock right out in the hallway. Charlie found it at an estate sale over in Westbridge years and years ago, and it chimes every fifteen minutes. It’s got this deep, heavy chime, you can hear it all through the house. So I always have a very good sense of the time passing by. 

I'll be sitting there, and I'll hear the quarter-hour chime, and I'll look down at the packet, and I'll think to myself, 'Well, I've been staring at this same page about French Impressionism since the top of the hour, and I haven't absorbed a single solitary word of it.' Because, like I said, I was busy thinking about the gutters or Dave's power drill or what have you. But I remember thinking those thoughts! I remember the whole ten or fifteen minutes perfectly well. I'm completely awake and aware the whole time. I can hear the neighbor's dog barking outside, I can hear the refrigerator humming in the kitchen... I'm fully present. 

There are no gaps at all, Doctor. I can account for every single minute. It's just that those minutes were spent... well, they were spent daydreaming about my chores instead of focusing on the museum notes like I was supposed to be doing. So, no, definitely no lost time or anything spooky like that. Just wasted time, I suppose you could call it!

inference.note: Ruled out F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder). Patient explicitly denies depressed mood, anhedonia, and emotional numbness. Reports sustained pleasure in museum work and no neurovegetative symptoms (sleep/appetite unchanged). Remaining symptoms are consistent with a dissociative or attentional disorder rather than depression. F48.9 (Unspecified Neurotic Disorder) best captures the persistent attention/concentration difficulties, possible mild dissociative features during routine tasks (autopilot driving), and avoidance behaviors without clear anxiety or depression.

doctor.question: You mentioned you hear the grandfather clock chiming and the neighbor's dog barking while you're reading. But I'm wondering—during those times when your mind is wandering and you're thinking about the gutters or the lawnmower, do you ever feel like the room around you seems distant or unreal, or like you're watching everything through a fog or a pane of glass, even though you know where you are?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of derealization (feeling like the surroundings are distant, unreal, or seen through a fog/pane of glass), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Through a pane of glass? Oh, my, no. No, definitely not. Everything is perfectly clear and real. There's no fog at all—well, unless you count the actual weather, of course. We get that thick fog rolling in off the lake some mornings, especially around late October, but that's strictly outside the window, not in my head! 

No, when I'm sitting there thinking about the lawnmower or what have you, the room around me is as real and solid as it always is. I can feel the exact texture of that brown leather recliner against my arms, and I can see the dust motes floating in the shaft of sunlight coming through the front blinds. Which, honestly, usually just reminds me that I need to get the Swiffer out, because Martha has a real eye for dust, you know. She can spot a speck of dust on the mantle from three rooms away, I swear she has eagle eyes. 

And as for the sounds, they aren't distant or muffled at all. When the neighbor's dog barks—that's a golden retriever named Buster, by the way, belongs to the Hendersons next door. They're a lovely couple, really, but they just let him yap at every single squirrel that runs up the big oak tree in their front yard. Anyway, when Buster barks, it's loud and clear right in my ears. It doesn't sound far away or like it's happening in another world. 

It's just that my brain is completely wrapped up in my own thoughts instead of the museum packet. But the room itself? No, it's perfectly normal. No glass, no fog, no feeling like things are unreal or distant. It's just my regular old den, clear as a bell. I'm just not paying attention to it because I'm too busy trying to remember if I bought the right size coffee filters at the Piggly Wiggly!
